description: Mongol successor state in Persia, Iraq, and Anatolia (1256–1335) established by Hülegü Khan after his sack of Baghdad (1258) ended the Abbasid caliphate; its rulers' eventual conversion to Islam under Ghazan Khan (1295) and patronage of Persian literary and visual culture launched the Ilkhanid artistic synthesis that shaped Iranian civilisation for centuries.

temporal.notes: Founded by Hulagu Khan after sack of Baghdad (1258); converted to Islam under Ghazan Khan (1295); fragmented after Abu Said's death (1335)

lifecycle_phases.description: Hulagu Khan sacks Baghdad (1258), executing the last Abbasid Caliph al-Musta'sim; destroys the Assassin strongholds of Alamut; advances into Syria but is halted by the Mamluks at Ain Jalut (1260); Ilkhanate established as one of four Mongol successor states

Persistent war with the Golden Horde over the Caucasus; intermittent alliance with Crusader states against the Mamluks; Arghun Khan corresponds with European powers proposing a Franco-Mongol alliance; court remains religiously pluralistic (Buddhist, Christian Nestorian, shamanist)

Ghazan Khan converts to Islam (1295), ending the Mongol pagan identity; reforms taxation, weights, and measures on Persian models; patronizes Persian literature and architecture; Abu Said's death (1335) without heir triggers terminal succession wars

rise_factors.description: Mongol decimal organization and combined-arms tactics overwhelmed Persian, Arab, and Armenian forces; siege of Baghdad demonstrated that no fortified city was immune
The Abbasid Caliphate, weakened by Buyid and Seljuk domination, had no effective military to resist; Persian regional dynasties similarly fragmented and unable to coordinate a defense

Mongol peace (Pax Mongolica) under Ilkhanate rule revived overland Silk Road commerce. Il-Khan rulers issued trading permits, maintained caravanserai networks, and reduced banditry that had plagued pre-Mongol Persia.

Ilkhanid rulers rapidly adopted Persian administrative traditions, retaining Iranian bureaucrats and promoting Persian as the chancellery language. This cultural synthesis stabilized a Mongol conquest state through indigenous expertise.

Hulagu Khan's sack of Baghdad (1258) eliminated the Abbasid Caliphate, removing the main regional counterweight. The destruction was so thorough that the Tigris reportedly ran black with ink from scholars' books.

decline_factors.description: Abu Said died without a direct heir in 1335, triggering a decade of civil war between competing Mongol clans that permanently fragmented the Ilkhanate into regional successor states
The Black Death (bubonic plague) ravaged the Ilkhanate's core territories from 1335–1347, depopulating cities and destroying the agricultural tax base

The conversion of Ghazan Khan to Islam (1295) was intended to win Sunni support but instead delegitimized earlier Ilkhanate rule while failing to reconcile the Buddhist and Christian factions that had been co-opted.
No stable succession mechanism existed among Mongol princes. After Abu Sa'id died without heirs (1335), competing claimants fragmented the Ilkhanate into regional successor states within a decade.

After the death of Abu Said Bahadur Khan in 1335 without an heir, the Ilkhanate fractured among competing Mongol and Turco-Mongol dynasties, Jalayirids, Muzaffarids, Chupanids, ending centralized Mongol rule over Persia and Iraq.

sources.author: Amitai-Preiss, Reuven
sources.title: Mongols and Mamluks: The Mamluk-Ilkhanid War, 1260–1281
